**One Hundred Years of Solitude**
García Márquez's 1967 masterpiece of magical realism, the defining novel of the Latin American Boom. It follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo, which first appeared in his 1955 novella Leaf Storm. The Colombian author won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and died in April 2014.

**Opening line: the firing squad and ice**
The novel begins: "Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice." The memory refers to a visit to the gypsies' fair, where Aureliano's father paid to touch a block of ice.

**Colonel Aureliano Buendía**
The founder's son, who leads and loses 32 armed uprisings in the Liberal-Conservative civil wars. He has seventeen illegitimate sons, all named Aureliano, who are later hunted down and shot through the ash crosses on their foreheads. In old age he shuts himself away making little gold fishes, which he melts down and remakes. His child bride was Remedios Moscote.

**Melquíades and his parchments**
The gypsy who brings inventions like magnets, a telescope, and ice to Macondo. He leaves behind parchments written in Sanskrit and in code that predict the family's entire history. They carry the epigraph "The first of the line is tied to a tree and the last is being eaten by the ants."

**The child with a pig's tail**
The family has long feared that incest would produce a child with a pig's tail. That happens at the end, when Aureliano Babilonia and his aunt Amaranta Úrsula have a son with the tail. The mother dies, ants eat the baby, and as Aureliano finally decodes Melquíades's parchments, a whirlwind wipes Macondo off the earth.

**José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán**
The cousins who marry and found Macondo. José Arcadio Buendía becomes obsessed with Melquiades's inventions and eventually goes mad, speaking only Latin, so he is tied to a chestnut tree in the yard until he dies. Úrsula, the practical matriarch, lives for well over a century and holds the family together.

**Other Macondo episodes: the insomnia plague, Pietro Crespi, and Remedios the Beauty**
Rebeca, an orphan who arrives in Macondo and secretly eats earth, brings an insomnia plague that makes the townspeople forget the names of things. The Italian pianola expert Pietro Crespi kills himself after being rejected by Amaranta, having earlier been engaged to Rebeca. The impossibly beautiful Remedios the Beauty rises into heaven while folding sheets.

**Love in the Time of Cholera**
García Márquez's 1985 novel about Florentino Ariza, who waits "fifty-one years, nine months and four days" for his youthful love Fermina Daza. Fermina married the respected Dr. Juvenal Urbino instead, and Urbino dies after falling from a ladder while trying to catch his escaped parrot in a mango tree. As a young man, Florentino ate gardenias and drank cologne to taste of Fermina and became sick, and he later rises in the River Company of the Caribbean.

**Jeremiah de Saint-Amour and the yellow flag**
Love in the Time of Cholera opens with Dr. Urbino examining the body of his chess partner, the photographer Jeremiah de Saint-Amour, who killed himself with gold cyanide fumes. It ends with Florentino and Fermina on a riverboat, the New Fidelity, whose captain raises the yellow cholera flag so they can keep sailing up and down the river together forever. Along the way, Florentino's 17-year-old ward and lover América Vicuña kills herself after he abandons her.

**Chronicle of a Death Foretold**
A 1981 novella in which the narrator reconstructs the murder of Santiago Nasar. On their wedding night, the wealthy Bayardo San Román returns his bride Angela Vicario to her family because she is not a virgin, though she had been advised to fake it, for example by staining the sheets with Mercurochrome. When she names Santiago as the man who deflowered her, her twin brothers Pedro and Pablo Vicario announce all over town that they will kill him. They do it on the day the bishop visits, even though nearly everyone knew, and Cristo Bedoya never manages to warn him. Afterward Angela writes Bayardo letters for years.

**"A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings"**
A short story in which Pelayo and his wife Elisenda, after throwing out the crabs that have flooded their house, find a filthy old man with huge wings, perhaps an angel. They lock him in their chicken coop and charge villagers to see him. Interest fades when a traveling show brings a woman turned into a tarantula for disobeying her parents, and the old man eventually grows new feathers and flies away.

**"The Handsomest Drowned Man in the World"**
A story in which the children of a seaside village find a huge drowned corpse covered in seaweed and jellyfish tentacles. The village women clean him, dress him in a sail, and name him Esteban. His beauty changes them, and they resolve to make their village grand so that ship captains will point to it in his memory.

**No One Writes to the Colonel**
A novella about an aging veteran of the civil war who waits for years for a pension letter that never comes. He and his asthmatic wife are slowly starving, but he refuses to sell the fighting rooster that belonged to their dead son. García Márquez was partly inspired by his own grandfather, also a colonel.

**"The Incredible and Sad Tale of Innocent Eréndira and Her Heartless Grandmother"**
A novella in which fourteen-year-old Eréndira accidentally burns down her grandmother's mansion and is forced into prostitution to repay the debt. Her lover Ulises, whose family smuggles diamonds inside oranges, promises her a new life and eventually stabs the grandmother to death.

**Of Love and Other Demons**
A 1994 novel set in colonial Cartagena. Sierva María, a twelve-year-old girl whose hair has never been cut, is bitten by a rabid dog and locked in a convent to be exorcised. The priest Father Cayetano Delaura falls in love with her and is punished by being sent to work in a leper hospital.
